title: The Combustion Science Database — Overview: the controlled fire
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Combustion is rapid oxidation that releases heat and light — fire, controlled. Engineers use it in engines, furnaces, turbines, and rockets, and spend equal effort keeping it where it belongs. The science spans chemistry (what reacts with what), physics (how flames propagate), and engineering (how to extract work and stay safe). This database is engineering framing only: fuels, reactions, engines, and safety — the knowledge that powers machines and protects people.

title: The Combustion Science Database — The fire triangle and tetrahedron
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat — the fire triangle. Remove any one and the fire dies, which is why extinguishers smother (remove oxygen), cool (remove heat), or starve (remove fuel). The fire tetrahedron adds a fourth: the chain reaction, uninhibited chemical radicals sustaining the burn — which is why halogen extinguishers work by interrupting the chemistry itself. Every fire-protection decision traces back to this geometry: which leg of the triangle are you breaking?
capabilities: Fuel, oxygen, heat: remove one, kill the fire
Smother, cool, starve: the three attacks

title: The Combustion Science Database — Stoichiometry and air-fuel ratio
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Stoichiometry is the accounting of burning: methane burns as CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, and the masses must balance. The stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for gasoline is about 14.7 parts air to 1 part fuel by mass — the mixture where all fuel and all oxygen are consumed. The equivalence ratio, phi, measures deviation: phi = 1 is stoichiometric, below 1 is lean (excess air), above 1 is rich (excess fuel). Engines run slightly rich for power, slightly lean for economy, and catalytic converters demand near-stoichiometric exhaust to clean it.

title: The Combustion Science Database — Flame types and flame speed
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Flames come in families. Premixed flames burn fuel and air mixed beforehand — the blue Bunsen flame, the flame front in a gasoline engine — and propagate at the laminar flame speed, centimeters to meters per second. Diffusion flames burn where fuel meets air at the boundary — candles, diesel sprays, flares — shaped by mixing, not chemistry. Turbulence wrinkles every flame, multiplying its area and speed. Flame speed data is catalogued per fuel, mixture, temperature, and pressure, because the same fuel burns differently in different rooms.

title: The Combustion Science Database — Combustion in engines: Otto and Diesel
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Engines turn fire into work with cycles. The Otto cycle — intake, compression, spark, power, exhaust — burns premixed fuel with a spark plug; its efficiency rises with compression ratio, limited by knock, the uncontrolled auto-ignition that rattles engines. The Diesel cycle compresses air until it is hot enough to ignite injected fuel on contact — no spark needed — and runs higher compression for better efficiency. The ideal Otto efficiency is 1 minus 1 over r to the (gamma-1), so a 10:1 compression ratio promises about 60 percent before reality takes its cut.
capabilities: Otto cycle: spark ignition of premixed charge
Diesel cycle: compression ignition, no spark

title: The Combustion Science Database — Deflagration versus detonation
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Deflagration is fire moving slower than sound: the flame front creeps through the mixture at meters per second, pushed by heat conduction. Detonation is fire moving faster than sound: a shock wave compresses and ignites the mixture at kilometers per second, with a pressure spike that shatters. Engines want deflagration and fear detonation (knock is its small cousin); pulse-detonation concepts try to harness it. The database records the dividing line per fuel and mixture, because the same mixture can cross it.
capabilities: Deflagration: subsonic, heat-driven, meters per second
Detonation: supersonic shock, kilometers per second

title: The Combustion Science Database — Fuel catalog
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Real fuel energy densities, the numbers that decide range: gasoline about 46 megajoules per kilogram, diesel 45.8, natural gas 55.5, ethanol 29.7, hydrogen 141.9 — the king by mass, punished by volume. Each fuel record carries its storage reality: gasoline as easy liquid, natural gas as compressed or liquefied gas, hydrogen as cryogenic or high-pressure challenge, ethanol as renewable blend. Choosing a fuel is choosing a trade between energy, storage, infrastructure, and emissions — the catalog lays the trade out honestly.

title: The Combustion Science Database — Combustion safety
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Safety is the other half of combustion engineering. Every fuel has flammability limits: below the lower explosive limit the mixture is too lean to burn, above the upper it is too rich — between them lies the danger zone (methane: 5 to 15 percent in air). Ventilation keeps concentrations below the lower limit; gas detectors watch continuously; flame arrestors stop flame fronts traveling back into tanks and pipes; electrical equipment in hazardous areas is rated explosion-proof. The safety record for each fuel names its limits, its ignition energy, and its required protections.
